name: ssh3
desc: Faster and richer secure shell using HTTP/3
why: Rebuilds SSH on HTTP/3 and QUIC, a genuine door into how a familiar protocol can be reimagined over modern transport.

brief.what_it_is: SSH3 is an experimental remote-terminal client and server, written in Go, that carries the SSH Connection Protocol over HTTP/3 (QUIC and TLS 1.3). You run ssh3-server on a host, with an X.509 certificate and key, and connect with the ssh3 client, which takes a user and host (plus optional secret URL path) and gives you a shell. It supports password, public key, agent, and OpenID Connect logins, plus TCP and UDP port forwarding. The homepage is an arXiv paper abstract; the README below is from the project's GitHub repository.
brief.why_it_exists: The authors say SSH dates from the late nineties and that they wanted to revisit it with QUIC, TLS 1.3 and HTTP/3, offering 'an enhanced feature set without compromise compared to SSHv2'. The README's main claims are faster session establishment (3 round trips instead of 5 to 7) and new authentication methods via HTTP authorization.
brief.how_it_works: SSH3 uses QUIC and TLS 1.3 to establish the secure channel and HTTP Authorization mechanisms for user authentication, mapping SSH Connection Protocol semantics onto HTTP. The server can sit behind a secret URL path and answer 404 to everything else, so scanners cannot see it. UDP forwarding uses QUIC datagrams, and proxy jump uses UDP forwarding so the middle host cannot decrypt the end-to-end traffic.

commands_seen.context: Installs both ssh3 and ssh3-server with the Go toolchain (the README's listed install method besides release binaries and source builds).
Builds the client from source in a cloned repo.
Builds the server from source; the README says this requires gcc.
Runs the server on a bind address with a secret URL path so it only answers requests to that path and returns 404 otherwise.
Starts a public server on port 443 with a Let's Encrypt certificate for the given domain, answering on /ssh3.
Client connects with a private key file and a secret path appended to the host.
Client uses password authentication, which only works if the server was started with -enable-password-login.
Config-based connection: the host alias my-server is resolved from ~/.ssh/config, and the URLPath option supplies the path.

brief.install_notes: Install with go install, use release binaries from the GitHub releases page, or build from source with a recent Go toolchain. The server build needs CGO_ENABLED=1 and gcc. There is no SSH3 daemon yet, so you must run ssh3-server yourself, for example in screen. The server needs an X.509 certificate and key (defaults ./cert.pem and ./priv.key). You can get one from Let's Encrypt (-generate-public-cert), use an existing cert with -cert and -key, or make a self-signed one with -generate-selfsigned-cert. Like OpenSSH, the server must run as root to log in other users. Server authorized keys come from ~/.ssh/authorized_keys and ~/.ssh3/authorized_identities. OIDC needs a ~/.ssh3/oidc_config.json file and a Google Cloud experimental app, per the README.
brief.standout: It keeps the SSH Connection Protocol but moves it onto HTTP/3, so the server can hide behind a secret URL path that returns 404 to scanners. Login can go through an external identity provider such as Google, GitHub or Microsoft Entra via OpenID Connect, with no public key copying. It also adds UDP port forwarding over QUIC datagrams, which OpenSSH lacks.
brief.status: Unknown in terms of activity. The arXiv paper was submitted 12 Dec 2023 (v1 only). The README describes an Internet-Draft, draft-michel-remote-terminal-http3-00, and notes the project 'is probably going to change its name' and that connection migration is coming 'soon'. I saw no release date or last-commit date in the pages I fetched, so the maintenance level is not confirmed.
brief.caveats: The README says it is experimental and a proof of concept: 'Do not deploy the SSH3 server on your production servers for now' and 'we cannot yet endorse its appropriateness for production systems'. Expert cryptographic review is still needed. The project may be renamed. Password login is off unless -enable-password-login is set. OIDC is marked 'still experimental' and needs manual setup. Reverse port forwarding is not implemented yet, and the client ignores most ~/.ssh/config options. There is no daemon, so you have to keep ssh3-server running yourself. The README's own advice is to hide the secret URL path but never rely on it for access control. I did not check the license.
quotes: SSH3 is a complete revisit of the SSH protocol, mapping its semantics on top of the HTTP mechanisms.
Faster for session establishment, not throughput !
Do not deploy the SSH3 server on your production servers for now
Your SSH3 public server can be hidden
